Shakespears's shortest play and perhaps his first comedy, the plot of Errors is nonetheless complex, showing early evidence of his sureness of touch and technical skill in knitting and unraveling complications. Aegeon, an elderly merchant of Syracuse who was parted by a series of dreadful misfortunes from his wife, his twin sons, the Antipholi, and their twin attendants, the Dromios, has been condemned to death by the duke unless he provides a ransom by evening. The two pairs of twins become entangled in an elaborate series of mistaken identities involving money, a necklace, a dinner engagement, the jealous wife and her unattached sister, a kitchen wench and a courtesan, to a point where they are assumed to be utterly mad or think themselves bewitched. In the end, as befits a farce, Aegeon is reprieved and the whole family is at last joyfully reunited.
